prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B021 first, but unanimity is not itself the argument. The argument is that this is a physiological discovery in the classical sense: the incretin effect, proglucagon processing into the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its insulinotropic and satiety actions in humans, and the receptor biology. That mechanistic chain was then confirmed independently in many laboratories and turned into drugs with outcome-trial evidence in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Maturity is not in doubt, and the scale of clinical use makes the timing hard to defend delaying. A three-person configuration of Holst (human physiology of secretion and action), Drucker (GLP-1 and related peptide biology, receptor and translational framing) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) maps onto three distinct, decisive steps. A single-achievement prize also keeps the citation clean.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for identifying the active peptide and its receptor is contested, and the supplied credit list omits contributors such as Habener who may have a claim that I cannot adjudicate from the provided text. Excluding Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, who led development of liraglutide and semaglutide, will be read by some as undervaluing the step that actually produced the therapies, and a citation that mentions treatment risks implying credit to the drug developers. There is also a risk of rewarding a commercially visible phenomenon over the underlying physiology. I accept that the three-seat limit forces a hard choice, and I would want the committee to test the decisive-contribution claims against the primary record rather than rely on recall, including my own.

responses.point: Perlmann placed B007 (antisense correction of SMN2 splicing) second, arguing that it converted a fatal infantile neurodegenerative disease into a treatable one and established splice-switching oligonucleotides as a modality, with a coherent Krainer and Bennett pairing.
responses.response: As a neuroscientist I am sympathetic, and the Krainer-Bennett pairing is cleaner than most. But I would not rank it above B022 or B012 on the present evidence. The therapy is recent, long-term durability is still accumulating, and newer SMA modalities complicate the question of what the prize would single out. The splicing mechanism and the chemistry are two distinct achievements, and I am not convinced one citation covers both without either diluting the mechanism or overstating the drug. I keep it outside my preferred configuration, but I would not oppose it as a later prize.

responses.point: Svenningsson placed B045 (BCR-ABL inhibition and imatinib) second and B052 (CAR-T) third, emphasising the paradigm of molecularly targeted therapy and the new class of living drugs.
responses.response: I agree B045 is fully mature and clinically transformative, and I ranked it eighth, not lower for lack of merit. My hesitation is that the attribution to Druker, Lydon and Sawyers is mostly translational, and the foundational BCR-ABL genetics sits with people outside the credited list, so the citation would be harder to word precisely than for B021. On CAR-T, I share your view of the clinical breakthrough, but toxicity, relapse and the unresolved Eshhar question make attribution less settled than for incretins. I would not move either above B021 or B022.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked B001 (cGAS-STING) second and B012 (TNF blockade) third, valuing the link to autoimmunity and interferon-driven disease and the fully mature anti-TNF evidence base.
responses.response: I agree B012 is fully mature and arguably overdue, which is why it is my second alternative and was third on my own opening list. I disagree on B001. The cGAS-STING mechanism is clear, but therapeutic translation is not yet established, and the credit list is crowded between Chen, Barber, Ishikawa, Sun and Wu, so a two-person split would need a careful look at who did what. For a prize that should show both discovery and consequence, I rank it below TNF blockade.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked B016 (optogenetics) third and B001 fourth after B022, treating optogenetics as an enabling technology with clear, original channelrhodopsin discoveries.
responses.response: We agree on B016's originality, and I ranked it fourth. My difficulty is the credit structure: Nagel, Hegemann and Bamberg identified channelrhodopsin, Boyden and Deisseroth deployed it in neurons, and Miesenbock's earlier work complicates the picture. A three-name limit forces an exclusion that could be hard to defend. Its direct medical impact is also still small, unlike B021, so I place it behind the incretin and unfolded-protein-response cases.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked B052 (CAR-T) second, just after B021, citing durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancies and a new therapeutic modality.
responses.response: I accept the clinical case and the multiple approved products, but I would qualify the ranking. Long-term safety, secondary malignancy, relapse and the absence of success in solid tumours leave the field still evolving, and the foundational CAR concept belongs partly to someone outside the credited list. That makes me prefer B022 as the first alternative, where the mechanism is conceptually complete and has been confirmed over three decades.

uncertainties: Priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide and its receptor, including contributors outside the supplied credit list, cannot be resolved from the provided material.
Whether the committee would accept excluding Knudsen, or would prefer a different three-person set that includes drug development.

Whether a two-achievement prize (for example the incretin discovery and a mechanism such as the unfolded protein response) could be fitted under the three-person limit; it cannot with the current credited sets.
My recollection of the discovery histories is from memory and has not been checked against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents co-authorship with Thomas Perlmann (a 2009 paper on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons), who sits on this committee, and with Sten Grillner (a 2019 review) and Patrik Ernfors; none of these is a candidate on the shortlist. No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from the provided profile, and shared institution (Karolinska Institutet) alone is not treated as a conflict.
